front.title: Redoubt/1: Authorised Control of Modbus-Era PLCs

abstract.t: This document specifies Redoubt/1, a control channel for programmable logic controllers that sits in front of Modbus/TCP and decides, per operation, whether a request may reach the controller. Modbus has no authentication, no authorisation and no replay protection; the TLS-based Modbus Security profile adds a protected channel but still lets any authenticated client invoke any function code. Redoubt/1 adds a decision per operation rather than per connection, a replay window that survives a controller reboot, a three-valued outcome that can drive outputs to a safe state instead of merely refusing, dual control for critical outputs, reversible batches, and an audit chain that fails closed. The decision core is formalised in Lean 4 and twenty of its properties are machine-checked; the proof artefacts are published with the implementation.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Modbus/TCP carries no authentication, no integrity check and no notion of who is allowed to do what. FrostyGoop, first described in 2024, was the first publicly analysed ICS malware that spoke Modbus/TCP directly to manipulate a district-heating process; the affected site lost heating for two days. In 2026 advisory AA26-097A described campaigns against internet-exposed PLCs from several vendors, using malicious project files and manipulated HMI data, and pointed at ports 44818, 2222, 102 and 502, that is, at the protocols themselves.

Two conclusions follow. Protecting the channel is necessary but not sufficient: a correctly authenticated client can still write to the register that stops a pump. And the component that decides what a client may do has to be as robust as the process it protects: available when the network is not, honest when its own parts fail, and able to say "put it in a safe state" rather than only "no".

Redoubt/1 is a guard that sits between the control network and the controller, a bump in the wire. The controller is unmodified: plain Modbus/TCP on the south side, Redoubt/1 on the north side. Every request passes seven gates in order, and a failure at any gate stops it:

ol.li: the frame authenticates and parses as exactly one known operation;
the frame belongs to the open session;
the frame number is fresh, given a 64-wide window and a persisted boot counter;
the policy allows this function, address span, unit and role, deny-overrides and deny-by-default;
for critical outputs, two signatures from two different keys;
the decision can be recorded in the audit chain;
the write is applied and journalled with the values it overwrote, so that it can be revoked.

section.t: An eighth gate runs on a clock rather than on a request: if the supervisor stops sending heartbeats, the guard writes the last-known-safe value to every output it has one for, and records that it did.

section.name: Conventions and Terminology
section.t: The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, MAY and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 .

dl.dd: a Modbus function code applied to an address span of a unit identifier.
the entity that terminates Redoubt/1 and speaks Modbus/TCP to the controller.
one of ALLOW, DENY and SAFE. SAFE means do not apply the request, and drive the affected outputs to the values provisioned for them.
the set of writes produced by one operation, with the values they replaced.

section.name: Threat Model
section.t: In scope: an attacker who can reach the north side, replay recorded traffic, modify frames in flight, hold a stolen operator credential, or tamper with the guard's own files; an insider who is authorised to operate but not to perform a particular action; a network that is unavailable or lying.

Out of scope: an attacker who controls the controller firmware; an attacker with physical access to the guard memory while it runs; a supply chain that ships a malicious image; traffic analysis resistance; and the security of the engineering workstation that produces project files.

section.name: Frame Format
section.t: A frame is one 24-byte header, a payload of at most 250 bytes, and a 16-byte tag. The header is the associated data of the AEAD, so a modified function code or address fails the tag rather than being trusted.

ul.li: version: 1. A different version is a different protocol, not a negotiation; there is no version negotiation.
flags: bit 0 RESPONSE, bit 1 CRITICAL, bit 2 DUAL.
session: the 64-bit session identifier from the handshake.
seq: the frame number, starting at 1, unique per direction.
addr and qty: the Modbus address span; qty is bounded by 125 registers.
payload: the values for a write, or empty for a read. A single write that requests dual control carries two bytes of value and two 32-byte signatures, 66 bytes in total.
tag: the AES-256-GCM tag over the header as associated data and the payload.

section.t: Function codes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 15 and 16 are understood. Any other function code is refused by name: a guard that forwards unknown codes forwards the next one too.

The decoder MUST refuse a frame that is shorter than the header, longer than the budget, of an unknown version, of an unknown function code, or whose payload length does not match the function code and quantity. It MUST NOT allocate memory to do so.

section.name: Handshake
section.t: Redoubt/1 uses the Noise KK pattern with X25519, SHA-256, HKDF-SHA256 and AES-256-GCM. Both peers know each other static public key before the first byte: provisioning already holds a list of devices, and a plant at three in the morning has nobody to ask.
section.artwork: initiator responder --------- --------- -> e, es, ss ephemeral, DH(e_i, s_r), DH(s_i, s_r) <- e, ee, se ephemeral, DH(e_r, e_i), DH(e_r, s_i) split two AES-256-GCM keys, one per direction
section.t: The prologue is the ASCII string REDOUBT/1 followed by the boot counter of and the device identifiers of both peers, so a handshake cannot be transplanted to another pair of devices or to another boot of the same device. Each handshake message carries a 16-byte tag over the transcript; a peer that does not hold the static key its public key claims fails at the first message.

After the split, the initiator send key is the responder receive key and the reverse. Frame numbers in each direction MUST start at 1 and MUST NOT repeat; a session that would exhaust its frame numbers MUST be re-keyed.

section.name: Replay Window and Boot Counter
section.t: A frame number is accepted once. The receiver keeps a 64-wide sliding window : a frame number above the highest is accepted unless it is zero, a number below the highest is accepted if it is inside the window and was not seen before, and everything below the window is refused.

A window in RAM is reset by a power cut, after which last week recorded frame is fresh again. Redoubt/1 therefore keeps an engineBoots counter, as SNMPv3 does with engineBoots and engineTime , in an append-only file in which every record carries an HMAC over the boots value and the previous record MAC, and links to the previous record. The counter is incremented and flushed before a session starts. On start-up the chain is verified: a record that does not verify, a chain that does not link, or a boots value that decreases is treated as tampering and the guard MUST refuse to serve. A truncation of the whole file is indistinguishable from a fresh installation, and for that case the guard compares its counter against a value held by the supervisor.

section.name: Policy Language
section.t: A policy is a text file of rule lines. Deny-overrides applies: a denial anywhere beats an allowance anywhere, and a request that no rule allows is denied. Order-dependent allow-lists are how people ship holes, so order carries no authority here.
section.artwork: allow fc in {3,4} addr 0..499 role reader allow fc 6 addr 40001..40010 role operator value in 0..1000 allow fc in {5,15} addr 100..199 role supervisor dual deny fc in {5,6,15,16} addr 0..99 safe fc 6 addr 500..599
section.t: A rule matches when every condition matches. fc is a set of function codes; addr is a span that MUST contain the whole requested span, not merely its first address; role is a floor, so a supervisor satisfies an operator rule and an operator does not satisfy a supervisor rule; value bounds the value of a single write; dual marks the operations that need two signatures.
A policy that fails to parse MUST be rejected as a whole: a guard that skips an unparsable line is a guard that silently allows something.

section.name: Dual Control
section.t: For an operation marked dual, the frame carries two signatures over the header and the value: one produced with the operator key and one with the supervisor key. Both MUST verify, and both MUST be present: a single signature repeated twice does not satisfy the rule, because the two keys are different and the signatures over the same input differ.

The signatures cover the whole header, including the session identifier, the frame number, the function code, the address and the quantity. A signature obtained for one operation therefore cannot be lifted into another: changing the address invalidates it.

If a dual operation arrives without dual control, or with a signature that does not verify, the verdict is SAFE, not DENY: an output that was about to be changed and cannot be authorised must be driven to its provisioned value, not left in whatever state the last authorised write left it.

section.name: Reversible Batches
section.t: Every applied operation records, for each address it touched, the value that was there before. The set of address and previous-value pairs is a batch, identified by a batch number. A revocation writes those values back and records the revocation in the audit chain.

The guard SHOULD keep at least the seventy-two most recent batches and MUST keep every batch that touched an output provisioned as safe. A guard that cannot record the previous values MUST NOT perform the write: an irreversible control action is indistinguishable, after the fact, from sabotage.

section.name: Audit Chain
section.t: Each audit record hash covers the previous record hash and the record own text. Periodically the guard signs the current hash with a key that is not stored in the log itself, producing a checkpoint. A verifier recomputes the chain and the checkpoints; a modified record breaks every hash after it, and a removed record breaks a checkpoint.

The log is a precondition, not a side effect: if the record cannot be written, the operation it describes MUST NOT be performed. A control action nobody can prove afterwards is an action that did not happen.

section.name: Dead-Man Timer
section.t: The supervisor sends a heartbeat over the same channel. If no authenticated frame has been seen for longer than the configured timeout, the guard writes its provisioned safe values to every output that has one and records the event. A guard that has never heard a heartbeat at all MUST behave the same way: absence of evidence is not evidence of safety.

section.name: Formal Verification
section.t: The decision core is modelled in Lean 4 and the following statements are machine-checked, with the axiom footprint printed by the checker (propext, choice and Quot.sound only, and no sorryAx): deny_overrides, no_allow_no_allowance, allow_requires_a_rule, dual_needs_a_dual_rule, no_double_accept, window_bounded, last_address_inside, payload_bounded, dual_payload_exact, boots_monotone, boots_never_decrease, dead_man_fires, dead_man_quiet, dead_man_fires_late, dual_keys_distinct, get_set_same, restore_previous, no_write_without_allow, allow_through_all_gates, denial_leaves_memory.

Of these, allow_through_all_gates is the one that matters most: an ALLOW verdict implies every gate was passed. The model is not the implementation, and the cryptography is an assumption rather than a subject of the proof; says so explicitly.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: This protocol does not make a controller secure. It makes the path through the guard decidable: unauthorised, replayed, unsigned or unrecordable requests do not reach the controller. It does not:

ul.li: protect a controller reachable by other paths, which is why the guard MUST be the only path and segmentation remains mandatory;
protect against a malicious project file that an engineer signs, which is the technique described in AA26-097A;
provide confidentiality on serial links at 9600 bit/s: the serial profile carries integrity and authenticity, and encryption is an optional profile;
defend against a compromised controller firmware;
replace key management, since provisioning, revoking and rotating static keys is out of scope and is where deployments fail;
claim side-channel resistance: tag comparisons are constant-time, the higher layers make no such claim.

section.t: The guard is a single point of failure by construction and SHOULD be deployed in pairs, with the two guards required to agree before a write is applied; a disagreement is a SAFE event.

The handshake has been cross-checked against a reference implementation of Noise: the initiator of this document completes a handshake with the snow responder and transport messages decrypt in both directions. Two deviations were found and fixed by that check, the prologue was hashed in two pieces instead of one, and the pre-message public keys were not folded into the transcript. Implementers SHOULD still prefer an existing Noise implementation to the reference code.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document has no IANA actions. It registers no URN namespace, no port and no media type; a deployment chooses its own transport binding.
